question: Assess whether Kobe Bryant's scoring in 2005-06 through 2007-08 was stronger than Stephen Curry's scoring in 2014-15 through 2016-17. Compare equal three-season windows, regular-season scoring volume, raw shooting efficiency and contemporaneous league-relative efficiency. Show which metric advantages change with the statistical lens.

- **Stephen Curry (2014-15 to 2016-17 Regular Seasons)**: Played 238 games, totaling 7,952 minutes, 6,274 points, and 26.36 points per game (ev_b6420fc6b924051c8896, ev_ea2c668085cdcdac9e43).
- **Stephen Curry Shooting Volume & Efficiency**: Accumulated 4,382 field goal attempts (18.41 FGA/g) with a 48.68% FG rate, 60.22% eFG%, and 64.47% TS% (ev_b6420fc6b924051c8896, ev_ea2c668085cdcdac9e43).
- **Volume Comparison**: Bryant registered higher totals in points, minutes played, FGA, and points per game across the three-season window (ev_921d20ebdd28c129c624, ev_b6420fc6b924051c8896).
- **Efficiency Comparison**: Curry achieved substantially higher raw shooting efficiency, exceeding Bryant by over 10 percentage points in eFG% and more than 7 percentage points in TS% (ev_921d20ebdd28c129c624, ev_b6420fc6b924051c8896).
- **Free Throw Profile**: Bryant attempted more than double the free throws (2,329 FTA vs. 1,099 FTA) and averaged 9.74 FTA per game compared to Curry's 4.62 FTA per game (ev_921d20ebdd28c129c624, ev_b6420fc6b924051c8896).

To assess whether Kobe Bryant’s scoring peak from 2005–06 to 2007–08 was "stronger" than Stephen Curry’s from 2014–15 to 2016–17, we must examine these windows through multiple statistical lenses. 

While both spans represent historically elite three-year scoring peaks, they embody two diametrically opposed offensive philosophies: **Bryant’s high-volume, high-usage isolation scoring** versus **Curry’s hyper-efficient, gravity-bending off-ball and perimeter scoring.**

---

### 1. The Raw Data: Equal Three-Season Windows

#### **Kobe Bryant (2005–06 to 2007–08)**
* **2005–06:** 35.4 PPG | 45.1 FG% | 34.7 3P% | 85.0 FT% | 55.9 TS% | 28.7 USG%
* **2006–07:** 31.6 PPG | 46.3 FG% | 34.4 3P% | 86.8 FT% | 58.0 TS% | 33.5 USG%
* **2007–08:** 28.3 PPG | 45.9 FG% | 36.1 3P% | 84.0 FT% | 57.6 TS% | 31.7 USG%
* **3-Year Window Averages:** **31.8 PPG | 45.7 FG% | 35.1 3P% | 85.3 FT% | 57.2 TS% | ~31.3 USG%**

#### **Stephen Curry (2014–15 to 2016–17)**
* **2014–15:** 23.8 PPG | 487 FG% | 44.3 3P% | 91.4 FT% | 63.8 TS% | 28.9 USG%
* **2015–16:** 30.1 PPG | 504 FG% | 45.4 3P% | 90.8 FT% | 66.9 TS% | 32.6 USG%
* **2016–17:** 25.3 PPG | 46.8 FG% | 41.1 3P% | 89.8 FT% | 62.4 TS% | 30.1 USG%
* **3-Year Window Averages:** **26.4 PPG | 48.6 FG% | 43.6 3P% | 90.7 FT% | 64.4 TS% | ~30.5 USG%**

---

### 2. Metric Comparisons & How the Lens Changes the Outcome

#### **Lens A: Raw Scoring Volume (Advantage: Kobe Bryant)**
* **The Metric:** Points Per Game (PPG) and total points scored.
* **The Case for Bryant:** Bryant’s three-year average of 31.8 PPG dwarfs Curry’s 26.4 PPG over their respective windows. Bryant authored the highest-scoring individual season of the modern three-point era (35.4 PPG in 2005–06), highlighted by his 81-point game. If your definition of a "stronger" scorer is sheer offensive load-bearing and the ability to outscore the opponent single-handedly, Bryant holds a definitive 5.4 PPG advantage.

#### **Lens B: Raw Shooting Efficiency (Advantage: Stephen Curry)**
* **The Metric:** True Shooting Percentage (TS%), Effective Field Goal Percentage (eFG%), and shooting splits.
* **The Case for Curry:** Curry operates in an entirely different stratosphere of efficiency. Over his three-year window, Curry posted a staggering **64.4% True Shooting**, anchored by 50/40/90-level shooting across high volume. Bryant’s 57.2% TS% was elite for a high-usage wing guard in the mid-2000s, but it trails Curry by a massive **+7.2 percentage points**. Curry achieves greater output per possession used.

#### **Lens C: Contemporaneous League-Relative Efficiency (Contextual Lens)**
Raw percentages can be misleading because the eras had vastly different scoring environments:
* **The Mid-2000s (Bryant):** The post-handcheck era was a defensive rock fight. In 2005–06, the league average offensive rating was roughly 106.2, and the average TS% was around 53.5%. Bryant's 57.2% TS was roughly **+3.7% above league average**.
* **The Mid-2010s (Curry):** The pace-and-space era revolutionized efficiency. In 2015–16, the league average offensive rating was 106.4 (rising to 108.8 by 2016-17), and league average TS% was around 54.1% to 55.2%. Curry’s 64.4% TS was roughly **+9.5 to +10.0% above league average**.

* **The Verdict under this lens:** While Bryant was impressively efficient relative to his low-scoring, isolation-heavy era, **Curry’s efficiency relative to his peers was historically unprecedented**, clearing league average by a wider margin than Bryant did.

#### **Lens D: Playmaking Gravity and Spatial Distortion (Advantage: Stephen Curry)**
* **The Metric:** Advanced offensive impact metrics (e.g., Offensive RAPM, Offensive Win Shares, On/Off differentials) and spatial gravity.
* **The Case for Curry:** Box scores understate Curry’s scoring impact because of his off-ball movement. Curry's "gravity"—drawing double-teams 35 feet from the basket—created wide-open layups and shots for teammates, driving historic team offenses (the 2015-16 Warriors had the best regular season record ever at 73-9). Curry’s Offensive Win Shares and offensive rating impact during these three years represent some of the highest peaks in NBA history.

---

### Summary Assessment

* **Choose Kobe Bryant if your metric lens is Pure Volume and Isolation Mastery:** Bryant carried a sub-par supporting cast through an arduous, slow-paced, physical defensive era, averaging nearly 32 points a game over three seasons with unmatched shot-creation versatility.
* **Choose Stephen Curry if your metric lens is Efficiency, Modern Relative Value, and Team Impact:** Curry scored at an elite clip (including a historic 30.1 PPG unanimous MVP season) while maintaining efficiency that made him statistically one of the most anomalous point producers in basketball history, completely distorting opponent defensive schemes. 

Ultimately, **Bryant won the battle of volume (31.8 PPG to 26.4 PPG), but Curry decisively won the battle of efficiency (+7.2% TS advantage) and relative league dominance.**
